Heists and Disasters

The Best and Worst Winters

  • Every club's offseason since 1998-99, added up: each trade at the club's own net over the control years, each signing at its surplus against what the money usually buys, in wins.
  • A winter runs November 1 through March 31. This is hindsight: what the moves became, not how they looked that day.
  • Winters from 2022-23 on are still open (contracts and control years are still running), so they are left off the all-time lists unless you ask for them.

Front Office Rankings · Active MLB Regimes

Pick any front office for its full report card.
The number under each Overall grade is the score, in wins a season. +3.5 means this front office's decisions have been worth about three and a half more wins every season than a typical front office would have gotten from the same moves; a minus means fewer. The letter is that same number on a grade scale, and the list is sorted by it. The bar beside it is the unadjusted total over the whole tenure.
How to read a row
  • Channel grades (Draft through Ret): wins above (+) or below (−) what a typical front office got from the same kind of move, per season in the chair. 50 is average on the 20-80 scale; A is about 70+, F under 35. Hover a grade for its number.
  • Overall is the ranking. The letter and the score under it are the same measure: wins a season above a typical front office, leaning on the channels where results repeat (free agency most, trades least), with a short tenure counted as if it began with two average seasons so one hot year cannot top the board. Net wins is the plain total of every decision's value in wins, before that weighting. Success grades results on the field; the gap between Overall and Success shows how much came from luck, payroll or inheritance.
  • Column key
    • Waiver / Minor: waiver claims and minor-league signings.
    • Int'l: international amateur signings. Ext: contract extensions.
    • Ret (retention): did the players a club let walk do more or less than departures of that caliber usually do?
    • Dev (development): prospect value created while the player was in the org.
    • Success: results on the field (win%, division titles, playoff series, pennants, rings).
  • SS small sample (under 3 seasons) · partial a channel with too few graded deals is filled at the league-average rate · · too few moves to grade (counts as average) · new too new to grade.
  • Every graded seat is ranked. Short tenures are partial samples and carry a small-sample tag; front offices hired after the last completed season have nothing to grade yet.
Where the numbers come from
  • Every value is Ledger WAR, built here from public data (park factors, defense, framing, baserunning), and only what has already happened on the field counts.
  • Free agency is graded against 2,766 guaranteed contracts; extensions against the league's extensions of the same service class; qualifying-offer signings carry the lost draft pick.
  • The Era filter adds 113 archive regimes (1998-2026), scored by the same engine over their actual windows. The full math and how well it holds up are on the Methodology page.
Accounting: realized results only (what has already happened on the field)

    Methodology

    Reading the numbers, in one minute.
    • Everything is counted in wins, using Ledger WAR, this project's own wins-above-replacement measure built from public MLB data. +2.0 WAR means two more team wins than a freely available player.
    • A decision's +/- is what the club got against what a typical front office gets from the same move: a trade at +3.0 brought back three more wins than it gave up; a signing at −2.0 delivered two fewer wins than its price usually buys.
    • Money becomes wins at that year's market price per win. Future wins in a trade are discounted 10% a year.
    • OPEN means players from the decision are still under club control, so the number can still move. Projections are shown beside open deals and never enter a grade.
    • Grades sit on the 20-80 scouting scale: 50 is average, 60 above average, 70 plus, 80 the very top.

    What gets graded, and against what

    The unit is the decision: a dated transaction, credited to the executive regime in office when it was made. Inherited players are not the new regime's; extensions, non-tenders and letting a free agent walk are decisions too. Each channel has its own bar, and a decision is graded only on the gap between what it returned and that bar.

    ChannelWhat the decision earnsThe bar it is measured against
    DraftWins in each pick's club-control seasons, every round, wherever he played themThe expected wins for that slot, centered by draft class (a late-round pick carries a bar of a few hundredths of a win, so a late-round hit is nearly all profit)
    TradesWins received minus wins sent, over each player's window, net of salaryThe other side of the same deal (zero sum)
    Free agencyWins produced for the club in the seasons it held the contractThe cost in wins x what a typical club gets in that contract year, on a deal that size
    ExtensionsArbitration savings in controlled seasons, plus production in the free-agent seasons boughtThe league's average extension of the same service class, per win of cost
    InternationalWins in each signing's control seasonsThe league's realized value per signing in that class
    Waivers / Rule 5Production for the club over the next three seasons (losses charged the same)Zero: pure found money
    RetentionWhat departed free agents did in their next three seasons elsewhereWhat departures of that caliber and age usually do
    DevProspect value created while in the org (top-100 rankings, 2011-26)League average, since development is positive-sum

    Net of cost, always. Free-agent signings and extensions never show raw WAR: signing a star who then plays like a star is a pass, not a triumph. Every graded trade, signing, extension and draft pick also shows its market comps: the three most similar moves league-wide and how they turned out. A trade is graded both as it looked at the time (prospects not yet in the majors carry their rank-curve value from the day of the deal, fading as real seasons replace it) and as it turned out.

    What a free-agent dollar buys, by contract year · wins returned per win of cost at market $/win, every priced free-agent season since 2006. Year one is roughly fair; by year five a club gets half. A deal is graded against these years, not against 1.0.
    The draft bar, by slot · expected wins in club control by overall pick (log scale). The first pick carries a bar of about ten wins; pick 38 about two. A pick is graded against its own slot.

    From net wins to a letter

    Each channel's net is turned into a rate per season in the chair, shrunk toward average for short tenures: rate = net / (seasons + 2).

    • The rate is read in units of that channel's own spread across every graded regime, then placed on the 20-80 scale, so A+ is about the top 5% of a channel and F about the bottom 5%, and a channel too thin to grade counts as average. Overall, the composite, combines the channels into one grade of decision quality and is the leaderboard's ranking.
    • Each channel's net wins count in proportion to how much that channel's results repeat (the second validation check below): weight = 0.5 + 0.5 x the reliability of the full record (Spearman-Brown on the split-half correlation), so free agency counts about 0.73, extensions 0.65, the draft 0.58, waivers 0.52, and trades, international signings and retention 0.5.
    • A channel that is mostly luck still counts, just less.
    • The Net wins column stays the plain, unweighted total. Success grades results on the field (win%, division titles, playoff rounds, pennants, titles) and is kept separate on purpose: a front office can out-decide the league and still miss October, or ride inherited stars to banners.
    • Each single move also carries a letter that ranks it among real moves of the same kind and size, so a $1M signing is judged against $1M signings.

    The value engine (Ledger WAR)

    • Every grade is in Ledger WAR, a wins-above-replacement measure built for this project from public data.
    • Offense: linear-weights run value, with park factors from each park's home and road run environments (three-year rolling, halved for the road split).
    • Defense: Defensive Runs Saved at first, second, third and shortstop; Statcast Fielding Run Value for catchers (framing, blocking, throwing) and outfielders from 2016; Defensive Runs Saved at every position for 2003-2015. Each is centered on the league average at its position every season, and positional credit follows the games actually played at each position.
    • Pitching: fielding-independent pitching (FIP: strikeouts, walks, hit batters and home runs per inning), park-adjusted and set against the league rate, times innings pitched, plus replacement level. Balls in play are left to the defense, so a pitcher is not charged for his fielders. Relievers are not credited for leverage.
    • Baserunning comes from public tracking data. Seasons before 2003 carry no fielding runs, only positional credit.
    • The cache covers 28,460 players, 1998-2026, and is checked for completeness every time the data updates. Whether it adds up is tested below.

    Who owns a season: control, contracts and money

    • Club control runs six seasons from the MLB debut (a debut after mid-April runs it one season longer). The decision that acquired a player (the pick, the signing, the trade) owns those seasons wherever he plays them, until a release or a free-agent filing.
    • One contract book holds every guaranteed deal the ledger knows: 2,779 free-agent contracts from the 1997-98 winter on and 826 extensions. A free-agent deal owns its seasons; an extension owns only the seasons beyond the player's original control.
    • Salary is charged at what that money typically buys: a free-agent season at the typical return for its contract year and size (so taking on or shedding a typical contract is neutral, and dumping the last years of a deal is not a windfall). An arbitration season with no contract costs the estimated award: (0.6 + platform WAR) x a class step of 1.0, 1.5 and 3.1 x the $/win drift, calibrated on 48 real 2026 awards (leave-one-out miss about $1.6M). A season lost to injury still charges the salary; cash sent in a trade is charged to the club that paid it.

    Trades: windows, discounting, and no leverage weight

    A traded player is an asset: the acquiring club is credited with his window (six seasons, or to the end of his club control if later) wherever he plays it, so a quick flip is graded in the flip.

    • Future seasons discount 10% a year from the first season of the window, the same for both sides; an October-December deal starts with the next season.
    • Trades are not weighted by playoff leverage: a leverage weight would bill the selling club at the buyer's leverage and move value from bad clubs to good ones by construction (seats on clubs under 72 wins would net −375 wins with such a weight, +33 without).
    • The exclusive right to extend an acquired player is a real asset too: once exercised, the extension's realized surplus is shown beside the trade, and a club that let a star walk is charged the surplus it forfeited, net of the compensation pick.

    Extensions

    An extension is graded against the path it replaced.

    • In seasons the club already controlled, the production belongs to whoever acquired the player; the extension only changes the bill, so it is credited the arbitration salary it replaced (the minimum in pre-arbitration years) and charged its own.
    • In the free-agent seasons it buys, it is a free-agent deal, graded like one.
    • Each service class (pre-debut, early career, arbitration, veteran) is then centered on the league's average result per win of cost for that class, so a club is graded on whom it locked up and at what price, not on which kind of extension it prefers.

    The salary follows the schedule these deals are paid on. Extensions are back-loaded: a few million a year before arbitration, more in arbitration, the bulk in the free-agent years. Charging the average salary every season would make every young player's extension read as a loss in its early years, so the guaranteed total is spread over the seasons in proportion to what each would have cost on the path it replaced (twice the minimum before arbitration, the award model for a 3-win regular or better in arbitration, the average salary in free agency), fixed at signing. Deals still running show a projected finish beside the grade, never in it.

    How an extension is charged, season by season · the same guaranteed total, spread on the schedule these deals are paid on instead of a flat average.

    Retention, conditioned on who left

    Raw leakage (wins departed free agents produce elsewhere) scales with how many stars a club employs, so it would grade payroll, not decisions.

    • The channel conditions on who left: from every free-agent departure 1998-2023 whose next three seasons are all on the books (2,827 with real value behind them), an empirical curve says what departures of each caliber go on to do over their next three seasons (a 2-win departure about 1.5, a 10-win departure about 5.8), adjusted for age (36 and older about half the curve; 29 and under about 1.27x).
    • A regime is graded on the gap between its departures' actual next three seasons and that expectation, plus +1.0 win for each player who declined its qualifying offer and signed elsewhere (the signing club carries the matching charge; the QO table covers 2012-13 through 2025-26).
    • Re-signings are not departures: a player who re-signs (or is extended before he files) is graded as that signing or extension. A deadline rental's walk belongs to the trade that brought him in: the trade was credited only with the weeks he had left, so charging the walk again would count it twice.
    • Departures through the 2025-26 winter are graded. A 2024 departure has two seasons to read and a 2025 departure one, so its expectation is cut to the share of a three-year total that departures usually deliver in that many seasons. This winter's departures have nothing to read yet.

    Player development (DEV)

    Prospects are marked to market on a rank-to-surplus-wins curve from the top-100 rankings archive (2011-2026, 1,548 rank-rows), with the holding org taken from minor-league rosters.

    • Entry credit is net of acquisition cost; a prospect developed to the list under a predecessor earns the new regime nothing at entry.
    • Rank moves accrue to the org holding the player, graduation is a neutral exit, falling off without debuting is charged, and credit stays home when the prospect is later traded.
    • Grades are league-relative (about +2.5 wins of prospect value per club-season league-wide).

    Projections (shown, never graded)

    Open deals show a projected finish beside the realized grade.

    • The projection is self-built: rate x playing time, then aged forward. Each piece was kept only if it beat the alternative on seasons it had not seen.
      • Rate. WAR per plate appearance (per inning for pitchers) over the last three seasons, weighted 5/3/2 and regressed toward his role's league rate by sample size. After a big drop or jump the same weights still win: in Ledger terms, breakouts and collapses carry forward about as much as the weights already assume.
      • Playing time, hitters. A regression fit on 2016-26 seasons: the last three seasons' plate appearances and games, plate appearances per game he was healthy (injured-list time from the transaction record), age and the rate. Games matter beside plate appearances because a regular sliding into a part-time or platoon role keeps playing games with fewer trips to the plate in each. Against the old formula it cuts the miss on next-season plate appearances by 11% (177 to 157) and removes most of the over-projection of hitters 31 and older (+78 to +9). Injured-list history, platoon splits and second-half role were tested and added nothing once those are in.
      • Playing time, pitchers. Starters 27 and older are pulled 15% toward half a season, trimmed when recent performance was weak, and kept to at least 70% of a full season just pitched. Relievers use their recent innings.
      • Aging. Curves built from 28,000 careers, with the decline set 1.5 times steeper than the raw year-to-year averages, which only see players who came back the next season. Later seasons also lose a share to attrition (injury, role loss, release) that grows with age. Checked against every regular and star since 1990, six seasons forward: for hitters of the 2010-19 seasons the projected totals land within 3% of what those players went on to produce, stars included. Stars of the 1990s and 2000s aged far more slowly than today's, so a modern star's projected decline can look steep next to memory. Pitchers land about 5% under.
      • Why an ace projects around four wins. The first projected season was checked the same way, on every season from 2016 to 2026. Starters coming off an ace year (5.5 or more wins per full season) averaged 3.4 wins the next year against 3.6 projected: some repeat it, and some barely pitch. Hitters coming off a star year (6 or more) averaged 5.0 against 5.4 projected. The projection is the middle of that spread, not a forecast that the player gets worse.
      • Hitters in their prime. Tested on every season from 2016 to 2026, hitters 30 and under who projected for 2.5 to 4.25 wins beat that number by about a third of a win, in year one and again in year two, in every stretch of years checked. Hitters 31 and older did not, and starting pitchers showed nothing reliable. So a hitter 30 or younger gets a quarter win added across a first-year projection of 2.75 to 4.0, fading to nothing at 2.0 and 4.75. Sixty-two hitters moved; no one else did.
      • Defense. Fielding runs count as they happened (Defensive Runs Saved in the infield, Statcast run value elsewhere), with no extra regression: in the Ledger's own record they hold up year to year as well as batting does. This is the main reason the projection disagrees with public systems on glove-first and glove-poor players.
      • Statcast read. For pitchers, fastball velocity, its change and contact quality allowed (wOBA against beyond xwOBA); for hitters, xwOBA beyond wOBA, sprint speed and its change. Fit on 2017-22 and tested on 2023-25, it trims the miss on next-season WAR by about 1% (pitchers 0.899 to 0.888 RMSE, hitters 1.567 to 1.551). Bat speed has only been tracked since 2023, too short to test.
      • On the page. Every 2027 projection on the free-agent board, the free-agent sheet, the simulator and each trade piece shows its playing time and its rate per 600 plate appearances (per 180 innings for starters, 65 for relievers), so a disagreement about playing time reads apart from one about talent.
    • How the Deal Desk prices a trade. Beyond each player's projected WAR:
      • Surplus, net of salary, over the years of control: projected WAR each season minus his salary in wins at that season's market price. Arbitration salaries for 2027 are MLB Trade Rumors' published projections (Matt Swartz's model) for the 294 players they list: on the real 2026 awards it missed by about $0.5M a player, against about $1.6M for our own WAR-based estimate, because arbitration panels pay on playing time and counting stats rather than WAR. Later awards build on the one before at the rate their model raises players year to year (about 27% of the last award plus $0.7M per projected win), and never fall.
      • Each club's place on the win curve: wins in the next two seasons count for more to a club near contention, so the same deal can read differently from each seat.
      • Roster fit: whether a piece fills one of the club's needs (a position below the everyday bar).
      • The market check: what real trades of the same shape (years of control, buyer posture) cost per win received, 1998-2023, with the nearest real comps and how they turned out.
      • Will it get done: whether the other club comes out ahead by its own lights, and each front office's record and tendencies.
    • Backtested by projecting each season from only prior data: r = 0.62 (2023) and 0.67 (2025) against actual next-season WAR, mean miss about 0.8 wins.
    • The same projections price contracts: for 1,434 free-agent contracts signed in the 2012-2025 winters, the suggested terms were rebuilt using only what was known that winter, and set against what each player actually signed for.
    The whole backtest, one dot per signing · Ledger offer vs what the player actually signed for, all 1,434 contracts 2012-2025, both axes log. Dots on the diagonal are priced exactly; hover any dot.

    Validation: does the metric hold up?

    Evaluating the evaluators. A site that grades front offices owes the same scrutiny to its own grades. Three checks, all reproducible from public data.

    1. Does it add up? A WAR-class metric must sum to team record. Across all 330 team-seasons 2015-2025, roster-summed Ledger WAR against actual wins above a 48-win replacement baseline: correlation 0.925, R² 0.855, slope 0.879, mean miss 4.8 wins. The slope below 1 is the replacement baseline and the gaps any WAR has (reliever leverage, catcher game-calling), left in rather than patched over.

    Roster Ledger WAR vs actual team wins · one dot per team-season, 2015-2025; the dashed line is a perfect match. Hover any dot.

    2. Is a grade skill or luck? Split each regime's decisions (regimes with at least six in a channel) into alternating halves by date and correlate the halves' average result across regimes.

    • If a channel's grade reflects a repeatable skill, a regime's odd-numbered moves should predict its even-numbered ones.
    • Free agency and extensions clear the noise (about ±0.2 at these sample sizes); trades, the draft and waivers show no measurable persistence.
    • These numbers set each channel's weight in the Overall grade.
    How much each channel repeats · split-half correlation across regimes (number of regimes in parentheses). Above zero means a club's good moves in that channel tend to come with more good moves.

    3. Does it predict? Pooled across 576 regime-years from 112 regimes (1998-2024), with decision value counted only as it had been realized by each season (no look-ahead), net decision value per season has a partial correlation of 0.15 with the next two seasons' W% after controlling for the record to date; the cluster-bootstrap 95% interval is [0.02, 0.28], and under grouped 5-fold cross-validation it adds a little out of sample too (R² 0.175 without it, 0.186 with it). That is small by design: next year's record is mostly the talent and payroll already on hand, which the record to date already carries. The question is only whether good decisions add anything on top, and they do, modestly.

    What the letters mean. The letters are an accounting of results: what the decisions returned against what a typical club gets from the same move.

    • They add up, and in free agency they repeat.
    • In trades, the draft and waivers the results are dominated by outcomes no front office controls, so a great trade letter says the trades worked, not that the next one will, and the grades on their own are not a forecast of next year's standings.
    • That is also why short tenures are shrunk toward average.

    Championship provenance

    Every World Series winner 1998-2026 carries a computed roster ledger: core contributors (≥ 1.0 Ledger WAR in the title season) traced to how the club acquired them, split into the sitting regime's moves and what it inherited.

    • Across all 29 titles the median champion was 55% built by its sitting regime, in year 5 of the tenure.
    • Free agency has been the majority channel exactly once (the 2009 Yankees).
    • The median title core was 52% self-built in 1998-2009 and 72% in 2010-2026, yet 7 of the 17 titles since 2010 were won on majority-inherited cores.
